place.en: Black Pine Ridge · the stream at the valley mouth

setup.zh: 那头鹿还在谷口的溪边喝水：三百步，东北，顺风。明天就是立冬。爹站不起来，把爷爷的弓递给了你。
setup.en: The deer is still drinking at the stream by the valley mouth: three hundred paces, northeast, downwind. Tomorrow is the Start of Winter. Father cannot stand; he gives you grandfather's bow.

recap.zh: 你拉开爷爷的弓射中了那头雄鹿；银月撑着说完指路的话，晕了过去。
recap.en: You drew grandfather's bow and brought down the stag; Yinyue held on long enough to guide the shot, and fainted.

zh: 一头雄鹿低头饮水，角如枯枝。
en: A stag drinks, antlers like dead branches.
The bow is heavier than you thought.

story.zh:
一行人正要下山，银月忽然在小满耳边开了口。

⟪「那头鹿。」⟫

她的声音比方才更小了，小得像一根线，一口气倒像要分成三口来说：「谷口……溪边……在喝水。三百步，东北，顺风。」

小满脚下一顿，低声道：「你怎么知道？」

「本王是妖王。」

「你方才说，醒一回，薄一分——」

她停了一停，才道：「……本王欠你一张饼。先还个利息。」

小满心里一跳。三百步，东北，溪边——昨儿晌午，他爹在山涧边上摸着的那个蹄印，比巴掌还宽，便是往东北去的。马三说的是立冬那天晌午。立冬，是明天。

他拉了拉他爹的袖子，朝东北指了一指，道：「爹。鹿。」

他爹瞧着他，没有动。老周在旁道：「什么鹿？你怎么知道它在那边？」小满张了张嘴，想起银月那句「本王只肯让你看见」，便把嘴闭上了，又张开，道：「……先看风。」说着拔了一根草，举在半空。那草尖儿往他们身后歪，风是从东北吹过来的。他道：「风从那边来，带着一股骚味。是鹿。」

其实他什么味儿也没闻见，只闻见他爹身上的泥腥味，和老周的烟袋味。可他爹是闻了一辈子风的人，听儿子这么一说，愣了一愣，也仰起脸来，抽了抽鼻子。他闻了很久，久到老周都开始往门板上坐了，才低声道：「……是有。」那一刻他爹是当真闻见了，还是不肯让儿子的话落了空，这件事，只怕他爹自己也说不清。

老周拦他：「你那腿——」他爹道：「明天立冬。」老周便不拦了，叹了口气，叫那两个后生扛着门板在坡上等着，他自己把烟袋往腰里一别，跟了上来。

三人摸过去。从那道坡往东北，是一道缓缓的斜坡，坡上长满了半人高的枯草，草底下是松软的腐叶。老周的脚步很重，踩断了一根枯枝，「咔嚓」一声，小满他爹回头瞪了他一眼，老周便把两只鞋脱了，拎在手里，光着脚走。走满三百步，只听得水声潺潺，小满伏在一丛灌木后面，拨开枝叶往外一看，果然是一道溪，溪边一头雄鹿正低着头喝水。

小满这辈子没见过那样的鹿。它比他家那扇门还高，身上的毛是赭红的，油光水滑，太阳底下一照，亮得像一块缎子。它头上那对角，像一丛冬天的枯树枝，枝枝杈杈，数也数不清。它喝一口水，便抬起头来，竖着两只耳朵往四下里听一听，又低下头去喝一口。

他爹伏在他身边，看了那头鹿一眼，呼吸便粗了。他解下背上的弓，搭上了箭，要站起来——却站不起来。他那条左腿在坡上趴了一夜，又在崖上吊了半晌，这时候又冷又僵，像一根冻透了的柴火，他撑着地使了两回劲，膝盖只是「咯」地响了一声，身子却一寸也没抬起来。他咬着牙，想换个法子，跪着射——左膝一沾地，整张脸便白了，白得像溪边那几块石头。老周伸手要来扶，他爹摆了摆手。

那头鹿又抬起头来，竖着耳朵听。风从它那边吹过来，它闻不见人，可它听得见，老周的喘气声太响了。

小满低声道：「爹。我来。」

他爹看着他。看了很久，久到那头鹿又低下头去喝了两口水。然后他把爷爷的弓，递给了儿子。

那弓比小满想的沉得多。

他摸过它不知多少回了，数过弓背上缠了几道牛筋——十七道，跟家里的盆一样多——可从来没有拉过它。它挂在墙上的时候，瞧着不过是一根弯木头，拿在手里，才知道它是活的。那弓背是一整根老桑木削的，拿手一握，沉甸甸的，凉丝丝的，里头好像藏着一股劲，在一下一下地往外顶。他左手握弓，那只手腕还肿着，一握弓把，疼得眼前一黑，险些叫出声来。他把那口气咽了回去，搭上箭，右手勾住弓弦，往后拉。

弓弦是牛筋拧的，勒进手指头里，像勒进了一块豆腐。拉到一半，胳膊便开始打颤，颤得那支箭在弓背上一跳一跳的，箭头对着那头鹿，一会儿对着它的脖子，一会儿对着它的屁股，一会儿又对着它头上那丛枯树枝，好像拿不定主意，到底该射它哪儿。他又往后拉了一寸，左手腕里「喀」的一声轻响，只觉得一股酸疼从手腕一直窜到了肩膀。

他爹在身后轻声道：「先看风。」

小满看风。溪边的芦草一阵往这边倒，一阵又直起来。风是一阵一阵的。他爹说过，风一阵一阵的，便等它歇一口气。他等着。胳膊在抖，手腕在疼，那头鹿喝饱了水，正在溪边的石头上蹭它的角，蹭得「咯吱咯吱」响，随时都要走。他还是等着。风刮过来，芦草一齐伏倒；风过去了，芦草晃了两晃，慢慢地直起来——
story.en:
They were just starting down when Yinyue spoke in Xiaoman's ear.

⟪"The deer."⟫

Her voice was smaller than before, thin as a thread, as though one breath had to be split into three: "By the valley mouth… the stream… drinking. Three hundred paces, northeast, downwind."

Xiaoman missed a step. Low: "How do you know?"

"This king is a demon king."

"You said just now — every time you wake, a little thinner —"

She paused before she said: "…This king owes you a flatbread. Here's some interest first."

Xiaoman's heart jumped. Three hundred paces, northeast, by the stream — yesterday noon, the hoofprint his father had felt by the stream, wider than a palm, had led northeast. Ma San had said noon on the Start of Winter. The Start of Winter was tomorrow.

He tugged his father's sleeve and pointed northeast. "Dad. Deer."

His father looked at him and didn't move. Old Zhou said, "What deer? How do you know it's over there?" Xiaoman opened his mouth, remembered Yinyue's "this king lets only you see me," shut it, opened it again, and said, "…Read the wind first." He plucked a blade of grass and held it up. The tip leaned back behind them; the wind was blowing from the northeast. "The wind's coming from there, with a musky smell. It's deer."

In fact he smelled nothing at all but the mud on his father and Old Zhou's pipe. But his father had been smelling the wind his whole life; at his son's words he paused, then lifted his face too and sniffed. He sniffed a long time, so long that Old Zhou had started to sit down on the door-plank, before he said quietly, "…There is." Whether his father really smelled it at that moment, or only wouldn't let his son's words fall empty, his father himself could probably not have said.

Old Zhou tried to stop him: "That leg of yours —" His father said, "The Start of Winter is tomorrow." Old Zhou stopped arguing, sighed, told the two young men to wait on the slope with the door-plank, tucked his pipe into his belt, and followed.

The three of them crept over. Northeast of the slope ran a gentle incline thick with dead grass half a man high, soft leaf-mould underneath. Old Zhou's tread was heavy; he snapped a dead twig — *crack* — and Xiaoman's father turned and glared at him, so Old Zhou took off both shoes and carried them, walking barefoot. After three hundred paces there was the sound of running water; Xiaoman lay behind a bush and parted the leaves: a stream, and by it a stag with its head down, drinking.

Xiaoman had never seen a deer like it. It stood taller than the door at home, its coat russet, glossy, gleaming like satin in the sun. The antlers on its head were like a thicket of winter branches, fork on fork, past counting. It drank a mouthful, raised its head, ears up, listening all round, lowered its head and drank again.

His father lay beside him, took one look at the deer, and his breath came heavy. He unslung the bow, nocked an arrow, and went to stand — and couldn't. His left leg, after a night lying on the slope and then a long while hanging from the cliff, was cold and stiff as a frozen log; he pushed off the ground twice, and the knee only gave a *clack*, and his body didn't rise an inch. He set his teeth and tried another way — to shoot kneeling; the moment his left knee touched the ground his whole face went white, white as the stones by the stream. Old Zhou reached out to help him up; his father waved him off.

The deer raised its head again, ears up. The wind blew from its side; it couldn't smell them, but it could hear, and Old Zhou was breathing too loud.

Xiaoman said low: "Dad. Let me."

His father looked at him. Looked a long time, so long the deer lowered its head and drank twice more. Then he handed his son the grandfather's bow.

The bow was much heavier than Xiaoman had imagined.

He had stroked it more times than he could count, counted the sinew bindings on its back — seventeen, as many as the basins at home — but never once drawn it. Hanging on the wall it looked like nothing but a bent stick; in the hand, he knew it was alive. The back was carved from a single length of old mulberry; gripped, it was heavy and cool, as if a strength were hidden inside, pushing outward, beat after beat. He held the bow in his left hand, and that wrist was still swollen; the moment he gripped the handle the pain turned his sight black and he almost cried out. He swallowed the breath back, nocked the arrow, hooked the string with his right hand, and drew.

The string was twisted sinew; it cut into his fingers as into tofu. Halfway drawn his arm began to shake, shaking the arrow on the bow so that the head pointed now at the deer's neck, now at its rump, now at the thicket of winter branches on its head, as if it couldn't make up its mind where to shoot. He drew another inch, and something in his left wrist went *click*, and a sour ache shot from wrist to shoulder.

His father said softly behind him: "Read the wind first."

Xiaoman read the wind. The reeds by the stream bent this way in gusts, then straightened again. The wind was gusting. His father had said: when the wind comes in gusts, wait for it to catch its breath. He waited. His arm shook, his wrist ached; the deer had drunk its fill and was rubbing its antlers on a rock by the stream, *creak, creak*, ready to go at any moment. He still waited. A gust came, and the reeds all bowed; the gust passed, and the reeds swayed twice and slowly began to straighten —

label.en: Half an inch to the left

exits.means: aims a little left for the wind, as told, and shoots

story.zh:
便在这时，银月在他耳边道：⟪「往左偏半寸。」⟫

她的声音很轻，很累，像是从很远很远的地方飘过来的。小满往左偏了半寸。

芦草将直未直。他手指一松。

那箭已离弦而去，「嗖」的一声，他还没瞧清它飞到了哪里，只觉得肩膀上一轻。那只小银狐从他脖子上滑了下来，软软地往下掉。他扔了弓，一把把它接住了——它闭着眼睛，身子凉得像一块冰。昨儿夜里它是烫的，烫的至少还是活的；这时候它是凉的，凉得像溪里的石头。小满慌了，把它往怀里一塞，贴着胸口捂着，隔着那件补丁摞补丁的单衣，觉出它很慢、很慢地，还在喘气。

他张了张嘴。他想说「谢了」，或者「谢谢你」，或者别的什么，总之是一句带「谢」字的话。那句话已经到了舌头尖上，可它闭着眼睛，听不见了。

溪边那头鹿却没有倒。它脖子上挂着那支箭，猛地一跃，蹿过了溪，四只蹄子蹬得水花乱溅，一头扎进对岸的林子里去了。老周「哎哟」一声，拔腿要追。他爹一把拽住他，道：「别追。追，它跑得更远。」说着偏过头去，闭上了眼睛。林子里「哗啦、哗啦」地响，一阵近，一阵远，响到后来，只剩一下一下的，又重又乱。他爹那一双听得见三里外獐子踩断枯枝的耳朵，这一回听了足足一袋烟的工夫，才睁开眼来，道：「它跑不动了。顺着溪，往下走，二百步，有个弯。」

三个人顺着溪往下走。走满二百步，溪水拐了一个弯，弯里的浅滩上，那头鹿侧躺着，四条腿伸得直直的，那支箭正中它的脖子，不偏不倚。它是跑到这里，才倒下的。

他爹一瘸一拐地跑过去，那条腿方才还站不起来，这时候不知哪来的力气，跑得比老周还快。他扑通一声跪在鹿旁边——膝盖也顾不得了——伸手去摸那对角，摸了一下，又摸了一下，然后回过头来看儿子，笑得像个孩子。

小满也笑。可他的手一直按在胸口上，没敢松开。

老周瞧瞧那头鹿，又瞧瞧那支箭，又瞧瞧小满，咂了咂嘴，道：「一箭？」小满他爹道：「一箭。」老周道：「他射的？」他爹道：「他射的。」老周道：「他才十二。」他爹道：「嗯。」老周道：「你十二岁的时候，还没摸过这张弓。」他爹道：「我十四才摸。我爹也是十四。」他顿了一顿，低下头去，拿手掌一下一下地摸着那头鹿的脖子，又道：「他十二。」

他没有再说别的。可他说那三个字的时候，那个腔调，和他跟马三说「三爷」的腔调，是不一样的。

小满捡起了那张弓。弓背上缠着的十七道牛筋，有一道松了，他拿指头按了按，按回去了。

那副门板，到底没有白扛。一头鹿，照老周的估摸，少说也有三百来斤，四个人把它抬上门板，老周和一个后生抬前头，另一个后生和小满他爹抬后头——他爹非要抬，谁劝也不听，老周劝了两句，便不劝了，只把门板往自己那头挪了半尺。小满走在最后，背着弓，捂着胸口。胸口那团东西，一路上一回也没动过。

太阳落到山梁后头的时候，一行人走到了岭下的石渡。那是溪上一溜垫脚的大石头，石头上长着青苔，水从石缝里哗哗地冲过去。过了石渡，便是马家的坡地——马家的田，马家的树，马家的风。

石渡那头，蹲着两条黄狗，狗后头坐着两个人。小满一眼认出来，扛叉的那一个，便是昨儿在断碑前嚷「也姓马」的家丁。他站起来，把叉往石头上一顿：「哟，还真抬出来一头。三爷说了，立冬前黑松岭里射着的，也姓马。放下吧，我们替三爷抬。」

老周的脸沉了下来，那两个后生看看老周，又看看那两条狗。他爹把门板往下一放，张嘴便要说「是，是」。小满抢在前头，道：「大哥，三爷说的是哪一天来拿？」那家丁一愣：「……立冬。」小满道：「立冬那天晌午，三爷亲口说的，半个村子都听见了。今儿还不是立冬。大哥今儿替三爷抬了去，明儿三爷晌午上门，拿什么？三爷说过的话，大哥替他改了？」

扛叉的张着嘴，一时竟答不上来。提锣的那个在后头小声道：「三爷的话……是说立冬。」小满又道：「一言既出，驷马难追。三爷家的马，也追不回来。」扛叉的瞪了他半天，脸上下不来。小满便从他爹箭壶上解下那只瘦得皮包骨的山鸡——昨儿前山打的，一路挂到了今天——双手递过去，道：「三爷的鹿，明儿三爷自己来拿。这只山鸡，昨儿大哥说它姓马，是大哥的。」扛叉的接过山鸡，掂了掂，脸上总算有了个台阶，一跺脚：「行！明儿晌午，一两肉都不许少！」

这一关算是过了，下一关却是石渡。门板抬上第一块石头，好好的；第二块，还好；到了第三块，那石头上青苔最厚，他爹那条左腿一踩上去，膝盖「咯」的一声，身子往下一沉，门板那头便歪了，三百来斤的鹿直往溪里滑。小满扔下弓便扑过去，拿肩膀顶住了门板的角，冰凉的溪水一下子没到了腰。老周在前头吼了一声，两个后生死死拽住。那鹿在门板上晃了两晃，到底没掉下去。他爹跪在那块石头上，一只手撑着，好半天才站起来，道：「……没事。它话多。」

两条黄狗蹲在石渡那头，看着他们一步一步地过了溪，一声也没叫。扛叉的那个家丁，也一直看着。小满知道，今儿夜里，马三便会知道那头鹿有多大。

到得村口，已是傍晚。

老槐树底下，站着两个人。一个是阿禾。阿禾站得很是古怪：两只脚的脚尖，齐齐地抵在老槐树的树根上，一寸也不肯往外挪，身子却往前探着，探得老长，脖子伸得像一只等食的鹅。小满起先不明白她为什么这样站，后来想起来了——她娘不让她出村口，老槐树就是村口。她一只脚也没出去，脖子却已经出去了。

门板还没抬到跟前，她的声音已经飘过来了：「小满。你欠我的鸡蛋，现在是两个半。」小满道：「不对。」阿禾眉头一皱：「怎么不对？」

小满便原原本本地算给她听：「本来欠你半个——芦花鸡没下的那一个。昨儿早上又借了一个，利息是两个，这就是两个半。可那个鸡蛋，我没吃，我转手给了……」说到这里，他隔着衣裳按了按胸口，「……给了一个比我还饿的。转借是要加利的。三个半。」

村口的人都笑了，这一回笑的却是阿禾。她大约是做梦也没想到，这世上竟有人自己往自己的账上加利息。她张着嘴，好半天才拿指头点了点自己的脑门，道：「……三个半。记在这儿了。那个比你还饿的，是谁？」

小满道：「一只狐狸。」

阿禾盯着他看了半天，道：「那它也得还。」

小满低头对着胸口小声道：「听见没有？你也欠她的。」胸口那团东西，一动不动。

另一个站在老槐树底下的，是小满他娘。她两只手拢在袖子里，一动不动，像是站了很久。后来小满才知道，她从前一日天黑一直站到这一日傍晚，中间只回过一趟家，是去给灶里添了一把火——她说，万一人回来了，灶是凉的，那可不行。

门板抬过来的时候，村口已围了半个村子的人，一阵一阵地嚷：「好大的鹿！」「黑松岭的？」「人也回来了！」「两个都回来了！」嚷成一片。

他娘却不嚷。她从老槐树底下走过来，走得不快，也不慢，走到儿子跟前，停下了。她先看他的脸，又看他的手，最后看他那只肿着的左手腕。那手腕上缠着的，是他昨儿夜里给狐狸擦伤口剩下的半片衣摆，早给泥水泡成了一条烂布。她一句话也没说，把那条烂布解了下来，从自己衣襟底下撕下一条干净的布，一圈一圈，重新给他缠上。她缠得极慢，极仔细，缠到最后，打了一个结，那个结打得方方正正，跟她补衣裳打的结一模一样。

然后她转过身去，看小满他爹。他爹抬着门板的后头，脸上的泥还没洗，一双眼睛红得像兔子。两个人对看了一眼，谁也没说话。她伸手，从他肩膀上拈掉了一根松针。

就这么一下。

小满站在那里，鼻子里忽然一酸。

人堆后头，刘豆芽看了那头鹿一眼，一转身，要往马家那边跑。小满隔着人堆叫了他一声：「豆芽。半块桂花糕，够不够吃？」刘豆芽的脸腾地红到了耳朵根，脚下却没停，跑得更快了。
story.en:
Just then Yinyue said in his ear: ⟪"Half an inch to the left."⟫

Her voice was very soft, very tired, as if drifting from very, very far away. Xiaoman shifted half an inch to the left.

The reeds not yet straight. His fingers let go.

The arrow was gone off the string with a *whoosh*; before he'd seen where it flew, he felt his shoulder go light. The little silver fox slid off his neck, limp, falling. He dropped the bow and caught it — its eyes shut, its body cold as ice. Last night it had been hot, and hot at least meant alive; now it was cold, cold as a stone in the stream. Xiaoman panicked, stuffed it inside his clothes and held it against his chest, and through his patched-on-patched shirt felt it, very, very slowly, still breathing.

He opened his mouth. He meant to say "Thanks," or "Thank you," or something — some sentence with *thanks* in it. The words had reached the tip of his tongue, but its eyes were shut, and it couldn't hear.

But the deer by the stream didn't fall. With the arrow hanging from its neck it gave a great leap, cleared the stream with all four hooves sending up spray, and plunged into the woods on the far bank. Old Zhou cried out and started after it. His father grabbed him. "Don't chase. Chase it and it runs further." He turned his head aside and shut his eyes. In the woods came a crashing, *hua-la, hua-la*, now near, now far, until in the end there was only a thud now and then, heavy and ragged. His father's ears, which could hear a river deer snap a twig three li off, listened this time for a full pipe's worth before he opened his eyes. "It can't run any more. Follow the stream down, two hundred paces, there's a bend."

The three of them went down along the stream. At two hundred paces the water bent, and on the shallows inside the bend the deer lay on its side, four legs stretched straight out, the arrow squarely in its neck, not a hair off. It had run this far before it fell.

His father limped over at a run — that leg that a moment ago couldn't stand now found strength from somewhere and ran faster than Old Zhou. He dropped to his knees beside the deer — never mind the knee — reached for the antlers and stroked them, once, twice, then turned to look at his son and smiled like a child.

Xiaoman smiled too. But his hand stayed pressed to his chest, not daring to let go.

Old Zhou looked at the deer, then at the arrow, then at Xiaoman, and smacked his lips. "One arrow?" Xiaoman's father said, "One arrow." Old Zhou said, "He shot it?" His father said, "He shot it." Old Zhou said, "He's only twelve." His father said, "Mm." Old Zhou said, "When you were twelve you'd never touched this bow." His father said, "I first touched it at fourteen. So did my father." He paused, lowered his head, stroked the deer's neck with his palm, once, then again, and said again: "He's twelve."

He said nothing else. But the tone he said those three words in was not the tone he used to say "Third Master" to Ma San.

Xiaoman picked up the bow. Of the seventeen sinew bindings on its back, one had come loose; he pressed it with a finger, and pressed it back into place.

The door-plank hadn't been carried up for nothing after all. The deer, by Old Zhou's reckoning, weighed three hundred jin at the least; four of them lifted it onto the plank, Old Zhou and one young man at the front, the other young man and Xiaoman's father at the back — his father insisted on carrying and wouldn't hear otherwise; Old Zhou argued a couple of words, then gave up and simply shifted the plank half a foot toward his own end. Xiaoman walked last, the bow on his back, a hand pressed to his chest. The thing inside his shirt didn't stir once the whole way.

By the time the sun dropped behind the ridge, they had reached the stepping stones below the ridge: a line of big rocks across the stream, green with moss, the water rushing between them. Past the stones lay the Mas' slopes — the Mas' fields, the Mas' trees, the Mas' wind.

On the far side of the stones crouched two yellow dogs, and behind the dogs sat two men. Xiaoman knew the one with the pitchfork at once: the servant who had yelled "named Ma too" at the stele yesterday. He stood and planted the fork on a rock. "Well, well — they really did carry one out. Third Master said: whatever's shot in Black Pine Ridge before the Start of Winter is named Ma too. Put it down. We'll carry it for Third Master."

Old Zhou's face darkened; the two young men looked at Old Zhou, then at the dogs. Xiaoman's father set the plank down and opened his mouth to say "Yes, yes." Xiaoman got in first. "Elder brother, which day did Third Master say he'd come for it?" The man blinked. "…The Start of Winter." Xiaoman said, "Noon on the Start of Winter — Third Master said it himself, half the village heard. Today isn't the Start of Winter. If you carry it off for him today, what does Third Master take when he comes at noon tomorrow? Is elder brother changing Third Master's words for him?"

The man with the fork stood with his mouth open and found no answer. The one with the gong said quietly behind him, "Third Master did say… the Start of Winter." Xiaoman added, "A word once spoken, four horses can't catch it. Not even Third Master's horses." The man glared at him a long while and couldn't climb down. So Xiaoman untied the skinny pheasant from his father's quiver — shot on the front hills yesterday, hanging there all the way since — and held it out in both hands. "Third Master's deer, Third Master can come for tomorrow himself. This pheasant — yesterday you said its name was Ma. It's yours." The man took the pheasant, weighed it, found his step down at last, and stamped: "Fine! Noon tomorrow — not an ounce of meat short!"

That was one hurdle past; the next was the stones. The plank went onto the first rock, fine; the second, fine still; the third was the mossiest, and as his father's left leg stepped onto it the knee went *clack*, his body sank, that end of the plank tipped, and three hundred jin of deer began to slide toward the stream. Xiaoman flung down the bow and threw himself at it, taking the corner of the plank on his shoulder; icy water rose to his waist at once. Old Zhou roared up front, the two young men hauled with all they had. The deer rocked twice on the plank and, in the end, didn't fall. His father knelt on that rock, one hand braced, a long while before he could stand. "…It's nothing. It's chatty today."

The two yellow dogs crouched on the far side and watched them cross, step by step, without a single bark. The man with the fork watched the whole way too. Xiaoman knew that by tonight Ma San would know exactly how big that deer was.

By the time they reached the village gate it was evening.

Under the old locust tree stood two people. One was Ahe. Ahe was standing very oddly: the toes of both feet planted together against the tree's roots, not budging an inch outward, while her body leaned forward, a long way forward, neck stretched out like a goose waiting to be fed. At first Xiaoman didn't understand why she stood like that; then he remembered — her mother didn't let her past the village gate, and the old locust tree was the village gate. Not one foot had gone out; her neck already had.

Before the plank even reached her, her voice came floating over: "Xiaoman. The eggs you owe me — that's two and a half now." Xiaoman said, "Wrong." Ahe frowned. "How is it wrong?"

So Xiaoman laid the whole sum out for her: "I owed you half to start with — the one the speckled hen didn't lay. Yesterday morning I borrowed one more, interest two, that's two and a half. But I didn't eat that egg; I passed it on to…" here he pressed his chest through his clothes, "…to someone hungrier than me. Passing a loan on adds interest. Three and a half."

The villagers at the gate all laughed, but this time it was Ahe they laughed at. She had probably never dreamed there was anyone in the world who'd add interest to his own debt. She stood open-mouthed a good while before tapping her forehead with a finger. "…Three and a half. It's in here. And that one hungrier than you — who was it?"

Xiaoman said, "A fox."

Ahe stared at him a long while, and said: "Then it owes me too."

Xiaoman lowered his head and said softly to his chest, "Hear that? You owe her too." The thing at his chest didn't move.

The other one standing under the old locust tree was Xiaoman's mother. Both hands tucked in her sleeves, motionless, as though she'd been standing a long time. Later Xiaoman learned she'd stood there from dark the day before to dusk this day, going home only once, to put a handful of wood on the stove: if they came back, she said, the stove couldn't be cold.

By the time the door-plank came up, half the village had gathered at the entrance, shouting in waves: "What a deer!" "From Black Pine Ridge?" "The people are back too!" "Both of them!" — one great din.

His mother didn't shout. She walked over from under the old locust, neither fast nor slow, came up to her son, and stopped. First she looked at his face, then his hands, last his swollen left wrist. Round it was the half strip of hem left over from wiping the fox's wounds last night, long since soaked by mud into a rotten rag. Without a word she unwound the rag, tore a clean strip from under her own jacket, and wrapped it round again, turn by turn. She wrapped very slowly, very carefully, and at the end tied a knot — a knot square and neat, exactly like the ones she tied mending clothes.

Then she turned to look at Xiaoman's father. He was carrying the back of the door-plank, his face still unwashed of mud, his eyes red as a rabbit's. The two of them looked at each other, and neither spoke. She reached out and picked a pine needle off his shoulder.

Just that.

Xiaoman stood there, and his nose suddenly stung.

At the back of the crowd, Liu Douya took one look at the deer and turned to run toward the Mas'. Xiaoman called to him across the crowd: "Douya. Half an osmanthus cake — was it enough to eat?" Liu Douya's face went red to the ears, but his feet didn't stop; he ran faster.

refuse.zh: 风还没歇。先看风，后看鹿。
refuse.en: The wind hasn't rested. Wind first, then the deer.

exits.means: ignores the wind and shoots straight

story.zh:
小满没理那句话。风？风懂什么。他照直放了箭。

箭擦着鹿角飞了过去，「笃」地钉进了溪对岸的泥里，尾羽还在晃。那头雄鹿猛地抬起头来，往四下里看了看，没看见人，只看见一支插在泥里、还在摇头晃脑的箭。它喷了一口白气，倒像在笑话这支箭，又低下头去，接着喝水。

他爹没说话，从箭壶里抽出第二支箭，递了过来。他肩上那团银毛，很轻很轻地，哼了一声。
story.en:
Xiaoman ignored it. Wind? What does the wind know. He loosed straight.

The arrow grazed the antlers and stuck *thock* in the mud across the stream, fletching still quivering. The stag's head came up; it looked all round, saw no one, only an arrow standing in the mud, still wagging its head. It snorted a white breath, as though laughing at the arrow, and lowered its head to drink again.

His father said nothing; he drew a second arrow from the quiver and handed it over. The silver fur on his shoulder gave a very, very small *hmph*.
